title: Payment Services Supervision
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to authorise and supervise payment and e-money institutions, from safeguarding and fraud to open banking, instant payments and wind-down.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to authorise and supervise payment and e-money institutions: assessing safeguarding, operational and fraud risk, overseeing agents, open banking and instant payments, and preparing for failure and orderly wind-down.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a practical understanding of how payment and e-money institutions make money, move funds and fail, and the risk-based tools needed to supervise a large and diverse population of firms. Participants leave able to test safeguarding and operational resilience with evidence, challenge firms on fraud, agents and third-party access, and act early when a firm heads towards failure.
sections.What It Covers: The payments landscape and regulatory framework, authorisation of payment and e-money institutions, risk-based supervision, safeguarding, operational and security risk, fraud and authorised push payment scams, open banking, agents, distributors and financial crime, instant payments and stablecoins, and wind-down and failure.
Intended Audience: Supervisors, inspectors and authorisation staff responsible for payment institutions, e-money institutions and their agents
Payment system oversight, consumer protection and financial crime specialists
Policy staff, team leaders and heads of department responsible for payments and fintech
Learning Objectives: Explain how payment and e-money services work and how they are regulated
Assess applications and ongoing supervision of payment institutions using a risk-based approach
Evaluate safeguarding of client funds using reconciliation and audit evidence
Challenge firms on operational, security, fraud and financial crime risk
Apply supervisory expectations to open banking, agents, instant payments and stablecoins
Design an early intervention and wind-down response for a failing payment firm
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day workshops. Each module combines a technical briefing with case studies, group exercises and supervisory question sets, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's payments sector.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of supervision or authorisation is helpful. No specialist payments or technology background is required.
Core Reading: CPMI, Fast Payments: Enhancing the Speed and Availability of Retail Payments (2016)
FSB, Enhancing Cross-border Payments: Stage 3 Roadmap (2020)
CPMI-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (2012)
FATF, International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations (as updated)

modules.title: The Payments Landscape and Regulatory Framework
modules.summary: How retail payments flow from payer to payee, who the participants are, and how payment services, e-money issuance and payment systems are regulated and overseen.
objectives: Explain the payment chain and the roles of banks, payment firms and schemes
Distinguish payment services, e-money issuance and payment system operation
Relate CPMI, FATF and PFMI standards to the national framework
syllabus: Card, account-to-account, wallet and remittance payment models
Regulated payment services and e-money: what falls inside the perimeter
Payment institution, e-money institution and small registered firm categories
International standards: CPMI, PFMI and FATF payment transparency rules

modules.title: Authorising Payment and E-Money Institutions
modules.summary: How the authority assesses applications from payment and e-money firms, matching requirements to the real business model and spotting weaknesses before they become supervisory problems.
objectives: Assess a licence application against category-specific requirements
Evaluate business plans, capital, governance and safeguarding proposals
Identify common application weaknesses and gateway red flags
syllabus: Business model, programme of operations and financial projections
Initial capital, own funds methods and fit and proper assessment
Safeguarding, security, AML and outsourcing plans at the gateway
Group exercise: assessing a sample payment institution application

modules.title: Risk-Based Supervision of Payment Institutions
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in applying a risk-based approach to supervising payment institutions, drawing on published supervisory guidance in this area, including how to assess safeguarding of client funds.
objectives: Explain the key risk categories relevant to payment institution supervision
Describe risk-based supervisory approaches for payment institutions
Assess the adequacy of a firm's safeguarding arrangements for client funds
Evaluate operational and financial resilience indicators for payment institutions
Formulate a risk-based supervisory assessment of a payment institution
syllabus: Key risk categories: safeguarding, operational, financial crime, conduct
Why payment institutions pose distinct risks compared to banks
Published supervisory guidance on risk-based payment institution supervision
Proportionality considerations given the diversity of payment institution business models
Facilitated discussion: risk profiles of payment institutions participants supervise
How safeguarding of client funds is meant to work in practice
Common safeguarding failures: commingling, inadequate reconciliation
Verifying safeguarding through reconciliation and audit evidence
Consequences of safeguarding failure for consumers
Group exercise: assess a sample firm's safeguarding arrangements for adequacy
Operational and financial resilience indicators for payment institutions
Case study: a payment institution's risk profile under supervisory review
Case study: formulate a risk-based supervisory assessment of a sample payment institution
Recap: risk categories, safeguarding assessment, resilience indicators
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Safeguarding Client Funds
modules.summary: How safeguarding is meant to protect users' funds if a firm fails, the common ways it breaks down, and how supervisors verify it through reconciliations and audit evidence rather than policy statements.
objectives: Explain segregation, insurance and guarantee methods of safeguarding
Assess reconciliation practice, safeguarding accounts and audit evidence
Identify commingling, shortfalls and other safeguarding red flags
syllabus: When safeguarding starts and ends, and which funds are relevant
Safeguarding accounts, acknowledgement letters and investment of funds
Daily reconciliation, shortfalls and safeguarding audits
Case study: safeguarding failures revealed on insolvency

modules.title: Operational, Security and ICT Risk
modules.summary: How payment firms manage the operational and security risks at the heart of their business, from strong customer authentication to incident reporting, cloud dependency and third-party failure.
objectives: Assess operational and security risk management frameworks
Evaluate strong customer authentication and incident reporting
Challenge firms on ICT, cloud and third-party resilience
syllabus: Security policies, risk assessments and major incident reporting
Strong customer authentication and its exemptions
Cloud, outsourcing and dependence on banking and scheme partners
Operational resilience: important services, tolerances and testing

modules.title: Payment Fraud and Authorised Push Payment Scams
modules.summary: How payment fraud, including authorised push payment scams, is committed and prevented, how losses are allocated between firms and victims, and how supervisors use fraud data.
objectives: Explain the main payment fraud typologies, including authorised push payment scams
Assess fraud prevention controls, payee verification and transaction monitoring
Evaluate reimbursement, liability allocation and fraud reporting data
syllabus: Unauthorised fraud versus authorised push payment scams
Payee verification, risk-based friction and transaction monitoring
Liability allocation and reimbursement models for scam victims
Fraud data, cross-sector information sharing and supervisory follow-up

modules.title: Open Banking and Third-Party Provider Access
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how open banking access rights operate under payment services legislation, and the supervisory considerations for account information and payment initiation service providers.
objectives: Explain the open banking access rights established under payment services legislation
Describe the roles of account information service providers and payment initiation service providers
Assess strong customer authentication requirements in an open banking context
Evaluate API access quality and its supervisory relevance
Formulate a supervisory assessment of an open banking access arrangement
syllabus: The rationale for open banking and third-party access rights
Account information services and payment initiation services distinguished
Consent and data-sharing frameworks underpinning open banking
Market development of open banking use cases
Facilitated discussion: open banking developments participants have observed
Strong customer authentication requirements and their application to open banking
API access quality: reliability, availability, and the 'obstacle' prohibition
Common friction points between account-servicing and third-party providers
Supervisory relevance of API performance data
Group exercise: assess a sample API access arrangement for quality and compliance
Bringing access rights, SCA, and API quality assessment together
Case study: an open banking access dispute or quality concern
Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of an open banking access arrangement
Recap: access rights, SCA, API access quality
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Agents, Distributors and Financial Crime
modules.summary: How payment firms extend their reach through agents, e-money distributors and cross-border provision, and why these networks concentrate money laundering, fraud and oversight risk.
objectives: Explain agent and distributor models and the principal's responsibilities
Assess oversight of agent networks and cross-border activity
Identify money laundering and sanctions red flags in payment flows
syllabus: Registration, due diligence and monitoring of agents and distributors
Cross-border provision and host authority cooperation
Money laundering typologies in remittances, wallets and prepaid products
Correspondent and bank partner de-risking and its consequences

modules.title: Instant Payments, Payment Systems and Stablecoins
modules.summary: How instant payment systems settle in near real time, the oversight of payment system operators and access to systems, and the supervisory questions raised by stablecoins used for payments.
objectives: Explain instant payment operation, settlement risk and liquidity demands
Assess payment system oversight and non-bank access to systems
Evaluate the risks of stablecoins and other new entrants in payments
syllabus: Instant payments: settlement, liquidity and fraud implications
Payment system operator oversight and the PFMI
Direct and indirect access to payment systems for non-banks
Stablecoins in payments: reserves, redemption and run risk

modules.title: Early Intervention, Wind-Down and Failure
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining how payment firms fail, what credible wind-down planning looks like, and how the authority intervenes early to protect users and their funds.
objectives: Identify early warning signs of financial or operational distress
Assess the credibility of a firm's wind-down plan
Design a supervisory response to a failing payment firm
syllabus: Early warning indicators: losses, funding, partner withdrawal and complaints
Wind-down plans: triggers, resources, communications and return of funds
Insolvency, distribution of safeguarded funds and user communication
Workshop: responding to a payment firm in distress

related.title: EU Payments Regulation: PSD2, PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on EU payments regulation for supervisors and firms, covering PSD2 and EMD2 today and the PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation reform package.

related.title: Big Tech, Embedded Finance and Open Finance
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping supervisors to assess big tech, embedded finance and open finance models, and their concentration, conduct and operational risks.

related.title: Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenised Deposits and CBDCs
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and central bankers to assess stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs, and their risks to payments and financial stability.

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.

related.title: Agentic Finance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to understand and supervise AI agents that transact and make financial decisions, from agent identity to payments and liability.

related.title: AI Governance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' AI governance, model and fairness risk, and to shape the authority's approach to AI supervision.
